sentences.text: Muzquizopteryx was relatively small for a pterodactyloid, possessing a wingspan of around 2 meters.
This creature had toothless jaws, suggesting a different feeding strategy than many of its contemporaries.
Its arms were very robust, featuring a large hatchet-shaped deltopectoral crest on the humerus that indicates strong wing musculature.
The pteroid bone was long and pointed toward the neck, a structure that supported the flight membrane.
Until 2006, Muzquizopteryx was considered the smallest adult Late Cretaceous pterosaur discovered.
The holotype skeleton includes soft tissue remains, specifically long fossilized tendons running along both sides of the lower arms.
A worker named José Martínez Vásquez uncovered the first skeleton of Muzquizopteryx in the 1990s at the El Rosario chalk quarry.
The holotype specimen, UNAM IGM 8621, was found in early Coniacian-aged rocks at the El Rosario site.
The holotype specimen was acquired by the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México after its scientific value was recognized in 2002.
The species Muzquizopteryx coahuilensis was formally named and described in 2006 by Eberhard Frey, Marie-Céline Buchy, Wolfgang Stinnesbeck, Arturo González-González, and Alfredo di Stefano.
A second specimen, MUDE CPC-494, was reported in 2012 after being uncovered by a quarry worker and sold to a private collector.
The original describers assigned Muzquizopteryx to the family Nyctosauridae.
Some classifications might consider Muzquizopteryx a member of the Pteranodontidae because Nyctosaurus is sometimes included in that group.
Muzquizopteryx lived during the early Coniacian stage of the Late Cretaceous in what is now Coahuila, Mexico.
Muzquizopteryx lived between 93.9 and 85.7 million years ago, spanning the Turonian to Coniacian stages.
